title: Collections & Language Internals
scopeHtml: HashMap internals, equals/hashCode, core collections trade-offs, immutable collections, streams, strings, boxing, records/sealed and exception cost (Java 8-21; versions marked where they matter).

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what happens when I call map.put(key, value) on a HashMap in Java 8+. How does it pick a bucket?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: HashMap is the most-used structure on the JVM. Whether you can explain hash spreading, the index computation and collision handling shows if you understand the structure or only its API.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "HashMap is an array of buckets. put calls key.hashCode(), XORs the high 16 bits into the low 16 (h ^ (h >>> 16)), then picks the bucket with (n - 1) & hash where n is the power-of-two table length. If the bucket is empty it stores a node; otherwise it walks the chain comparing hash then equals, replacing the value on a match or appending a new node. When size exceeds capacity times load factor (0.75) the table doubles. A long chain can become a red-black tree."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Step by step for put(k, v):

  1. hash = spread(k.hashCode()) where spread(h) = h ^ (h >>> 16). Null key hashes to 0.
  2. Table is lazily allocated on first put (default capacity 16, load factor 0.75, per the Javadoc).
  3. index = (n - 1) & hash. Because n is a power of two, this equals hash mod n but is one AND instruction. It also means only the low bits pick the bucket, which is why spreading matters: without it, hash codes that differ only in high bits (e.g. floats, large Long values) would all collide in a small table.
  4. Empty bucket: create a Node(hash, key, value, next). Non-empty: compare the stored hash first (cheap int compare), then == or equals. Match: overwrite value, return the old one. No match: append to chain (tail insertion since Java 8; Java 7 used head insertion, which could create a cyclic list during concurrent resize).
  5. Chain length >= 8 and table length >= 64: convert the bin to a red-black tree (see the treeification question). Fewer than 64: resize instead.
  6. ++size > threshold (capacity x 0.75): resize to double.
table (n=16)
[0] -> null
[1] -> Node(h=17,"a") -> Node(h=33,"b") -> null     // both: (16-1) & h == 1
[2] -> null
...
index = (n-1) & (h ^ (h >>> 16))

Each Node is an object: with compressed oops it is 32 bytes (12 header + 4 hash + 3x4 refs, padded). That overhead matters at millions of entries (see the boxing question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static int spread(int h) { return h ^ (h >>> 16); }   // what HashMap.hash() does for non-null keys

int n = 16;
int h = new Object[0].hashCode(); // any hash
int index = (n - 1) & spread(h);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "index = hashCode % length". It is & (n-1), and that only works because length is a power of two (even new HashMap<>(10) rounds up to 16).
  • Claiming collisions mean different keys with the same hashCode only. Different hashCodes can share a bucket too (same low bits).
  • Forgetting that equals is only invoked after hashes match.
  • Saying chains are always linked lists in Java 8+ (they can be trees).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why h ^ (h >>> 16)? → Mixes high bits into the low bits used for the index, cheaply reducing collisions for hashes that vary mostly in the upper bits.
  2. Why a power-of-two table? → Cheap masking, and on resize each entry either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCap, so no rehash is needed.
  3. What changed from Java 7 to 8? → Tail insertion, tree bins, simpler hash spread, resize preserves relative order and splits lo/hi lists without recomputing hashes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "hashCode, bucket, linked list, equals." Senior adds spreading, the AND mask and why capacity is a power of two, lazy allocation, hash-then-equals comparison order, tree bins, per-node memory cost, and that all of this is an implementation detail the Javadoc does not promise.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that key maps by objects with poor hashCodes (see the hash-flooding scenario) discover that the structure only gives O(1) if hashCode distributes well.

questions.promptHtml: What is the equals/hashCode contract, and what actually breaks if you override one without the other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the classic fundamentals filter. Seniors are expected to state the full contract and show the failure in a HashSet, not just recite "override both".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "If a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and false for null. If I override equals but not hashCode, two equal objects usually land in different buckets, so HashSet.contains and HashMap.get return false for a key that is logically present. The reverse is legal but slow: equal hashes for unequal objects is just a collision."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Contract from Object Javadoc:

  • equals: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent (same result while compared fields do not change), x.equals(null) is false.
  • hashCode: consistent within one execution while equals-relevant fields do not change; equal objects must have equal hashCodes; unequal objects may share a hash (no requirement of distinctness).

Mechanically, HashMap finds the bucket via hashCode and only then calls equals. If equal objects hash differently, lookup goes to the wrong bucket and never reaches equals.

Typical subtle violations:

  • Symmetry broken by inheritance: Point.equals accepts ColorPoint but ColorPoint.equals checks colour. Fixes: composition, getClass() comparison (breaks Liskov for subclasses), or make the class final / use records.
  • Hash from fields that equals ignores (or the reverse): hashCode includes a mutable lastSeen field that equals does not compare.
  • Floating point: compare with Double.compare, not == (NaN, -0.0).
  • JPA entities with generated ids: hashCode based on id changes after persist while the entity sits in a HashSet.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
final class UserId {
    private final String tenant; private final long id;
    UserId(String t, long i) { tenant = t; id = i; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof UserId u && id == u.id && tenant.equals(u.tenant);
    }
    // Broken variant: omit this and equal UserIds go to different buckets
    @Override public int hashCode() { return java.util.Objects.hash(tenant, id); }
}
// Kotlin: data class generates equals/hashCode from primary-constructor properties only
data class UserId(val tenant: String, val id: Long)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• hashCode() returning a constant: legal, but turns the map into a list (a tree if keys are Comparable).
  • Using Objects.hash(...) in a hot path: it allocates a varargs array and boxes primitives (fine usually; measure on hot paths).
  • Using instanceof equals in a non-final class that has subclasses adding state.
  • Assuming hashCode is stable across JVM runs. Object.hashCode is not, and String's is only by implementation convention (it is specified for String, not for most classes).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a constant hashCode correct? → Yes, legal; terrible performance (O(n) bucket, or O(log n) with Comparable tree bins).
  2. Why not include a mutable field in hashCode? → The entry becomes unreachable after mutation (see the mutable-key scenario).
  3. How do records and Kotlin data classes handle this? → Generated from all components / primary-constructor properties; deep mutability of a component (a List or array) still leaks through. Record arrays use reference equality.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Override both." Senior: states all five equals properties, shows the inheritance/symmetry trap, covers floating point and JPA identity pitfalls, and prefers records/final classes so the problem is designed away.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cache keyed by a DTO without hashCode silently had a 0% hit rate; every request missed and hit the DB until someone noticed the cache size growing unbounded.

questions.promptHtml: When and why does HashMap turn a bucket into a red-black tree? What are the thresholds and what happens if the keys are not Comparable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the Java 8 change precisely (thresholds and the table-size gate) and can reason about worst-case behaviour, not just quote "8".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When a single bin reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the bin is converted to a red-black tree, giving O(log n) instead of O(n) in that bin. If the table is smaller than 64, HashMap resizes instead. A tree bin reverts to a list when it shrinks to 6 or fewer (checked on resize). Ordering inside the tree uses hash first, then Comparable if the keys share a class and implement it, and otherwise a tie-break that forces searching both subtrees, so non-Comparable keys with colliding hashes degrade back toward O(n)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Constants in OpenJDK HashMap: TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8, UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6, MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64. The gap between 8 and 6 provides hysteresis so a bin does not flip back and forth.

Why 8? The source comments model bin sizes with a Poisson distribution at load factor 0.75 (parameter about 0.5); the chance of a bin reaching 8 under good hashing is on the order of 6 in 100 million. Trees exist as a defence against bad hash functions or attacks, not for normal operation. Tree nodes (TreeNode) are about twice the size of plain nodes, another reason to avoid them.

Ordering in a tree bin: compare hash; on a tie, if both keys are the same class and Comparable, use compareTo; otherwise fall back to System.identityHashCode-based ordering (tieBreakOrder). Lookup on a tie with no usable ordering must search both children, so the worst case remains O(n) for colliding, non-Comparable keys. The Javadoc says the same in words: when keys are Comparable, comparison order may be used to break ties.

bin length  table size  action
< 8         any         linked list
>= 8        < 64        resize() (spreads the keys, avoid treeify)
>= 8        >= 64       treeify -> red-black tree
tree shrinks to <= 6 (on resize split)   -> back to list

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Colliding hashCodes, Comparable key => tree bin degrades to O(log n)
record Key(int id) implements Comparable<Key> {
    @Override public int hashCode() { return 42; }               // deliberate collision
    @Override public int compareTo(Key o) { return Integer.compare(id, o.id); }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the 64 minimum: a small map with a long chain doubles instead of treeifying.
  • Claiming treeification makes HashMap "always O(log n)". Only with distributed or Comparable keys.
  • Saying LinkedHashMap/ConcurrentHashMap do not treeify. Both do (ConcurrentHashMap uses TreeBin).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why 6 for untreeify rather than 7? → Hysteresis against thrash around the threshold.
  2. Does iteration order change when a bin is treeified? → Tree nodes keep a next chain, so iteration still follows insertion-ish chain order, but order was never guaranteed.
  3. Does this stop hash-flooding DoS? → Only partially: Strings are Comparable so attacks degrade to O(log n); custom non-Comparable keys do not get protection (see the hash-flooding scenario).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "After 8 collisions it becomes a tree." Senior: states all three constants, the resize-first rule, the Poisson rationale, the Comparable dependency, the memory cost, and that it is a safety net, not a performance feature.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Services parsing user-controlled keys (headers, JSON fields) rely on this net for P99 stability. Teams with custom key types learned the net does not hold without Comparable.

questions.promptHtml: ArrayList or LinkedList: which do you use and why? Is the textbook "LinkedList is faster for inserts" true on the JVM?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Textbook Big-O vs hardware reality. Weak candidates recite the table; strong candidates mention cache locality, memory overhead and when LinkedList is actually a fit (almost never).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Default to ArrayList. It is a contiguous array: O(1) random access, amortized O(1) append, O(n) mid insert via System.arraycopy, which is very fast memcpy. LinkedList gives O(1) insert only if you already hold the node/iterator position; finding the position is O(n) with pointer chasing and cache misses, and each element costs a 24-byte node. In practice ArrayList wins even for many middle inserts until lists get large. If I need a queue or deque I use ArrayDeque, not LinkedList."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ArrayList: Object[] backing array. Default empty then capacity 10 on first add; growth is oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1), i.e. 1.5x. Append is amortized O(1). add(i, e) and remove(i) shift tail with arraycopy. Elements are contiguous refs, so iteration is prefetch-friendly.
  • LinkedList: doubly-linked Node(item, next, prev). With compressed oops a node is 12 header + 3x4 refs = 24 bytes, versus 4 bytes per slot in ArrayList (plus the element objects in both). get(i) walks from the nearer end: O(n). Every node is a separate heap object, so traversal chases pointers and pays cache misses and more GC work.
  • Mid insert in LinkedList needs ListIterator.add at a position you already hold; list.add(i, x) still walks O(n) first.
  • LinkedList implements Deque, but ArrayDeque is lighter and faster for stack/queue use (no node allocation).
Operation ArrayList LinkedList
get(i) O(1) O(n)
add at end amortized O(1) O(1)
add/remove at index O(n) memmove O(n) walk + O(1) link
removeFirst O(n) O(1)
memory per element ~4 B ref ~24 B node + 4

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var list = new java.util.ArrayList<Integer>(expectedSize);   // pre-size to avoid grow copies
// queue / stack
var dq = new java.util.ArrayDeque<String>();
dq.addLast("a"); dq.pollFirst();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Looping for (int i...) list.get(i) on a LinkedList: O(n^2).
  • Using ArrayList.remove(0) in a loop as a queue: O(n) each.
  • Arrays.asList / List.of assumed to be ArrayList (fixed-size / immutable).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is ArrayList growth 1.5x? → Trades copy frequency against wasted space; with 1.5x freed old arrays can be reused, and amortized cost stays O(1).
  2. When is LinkedList genuinely better? → Rare: very frequent removal while iterating with Iterator.remove on large lists, and even then profile first.
  3. What does ensureCapacity/trimToSize do? → Pre-grow to avoid repeated copies / shrink the backing array to size.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: recites Big-O and picks LinkedList for inserts. Senior: cites node overhead, cache locality, ArrayDeque for queues, pre-sizing, and says the LinkedList-wins cases are nearly nonexistent in production code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A report builder using LinkedList for 5M rows with indexed access spent 70% of CPU in LinkedList.node(); switching to ArrayList cut it to seconds.

questions.contextHtml:
A session tracker keeps active sessions in a HashMap<SessionKey, Session>; about 40k entries, 800 RPS. After a recent change, ops see "session not found" errors for sessions that definitely exist, plus a slow memory leak: the map grows, never shrinks, and remove() returns null. Code:

class SessionKey {
    String userId; String deviceId;
    SessionKey(String u, String d) { userId = u; deviceId = d; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof SessionKey k && userId.equals(k.userId) && deviceId.equals(k.deviceId);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return java.util.Objects.hash(userId, deviceId); }
}

SessionKey key = new SessionKey(user, "unknown");
sessions.put(key, session);
...
key.deviceId = reportedDevice;      // device id learned later
Session s = sessions.get(key);      // null!
sessions.remove(key);               // no-op, entry leaks

Red herring: the team suspects a recent Tomcat upgrade and GC settings.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain exactly why get and remove fail, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Maybe a race condition, add synchronized" or "equals is wrong". The equals/hashCode pair is actually correct. The mistake is mutating a field that participates in the hash after insertion.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the map shared between threads (to separate this from a race)? Does the failure correlate with the code path that sets deviceId? Is remove ever returning non-null? Is the map's size growing relative to live sessions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop mutating the key (build a new key and re-put) or revert the change; for existing leaked entries, a periodic sweep iterating entrySet (which still sees them) removes stale ones.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key mutated after insert (hash changed); (b) concurrent unsynchronized HashMap use (would also corrupt, produce odd CPU, not consistent misses on one path); (c) container upgrade (unrelated); (d) GC/leak from something else.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump + MAT: find HashMap$Node whose cached hash field differs from hash(key.hashCode()). Unit test: put, mutate, get, assert. Iterate entrySet() and compare get(entry.getKey()). Check logs for the code path that sets deviceId.
  5. Root cause: Node.hash is stored at put time. After mutation, key.hashCode() changes, so get computes a different bucket index (and hash) and never finds the old node. The entry is still reachable via iteration but unreachable by key: a leak plus phantom misses.
  6. Fix: Make the key immutable (final fields, or a record) and re-insert with a new key when the device is learned:
record SessionKey(String userId, String deviceId) {}
Session s = sessions.remove(new SessionKey(user, "unknown"));
sessions.put(new SessionKey(user, reportedDevice), s);

Long-term: forbid mutable key classes via review rule/ErrorProne; consider keying by a stable session id. 7. Prevention: records/final for any map key or set element; a unit test per key class that asserts hashCode stability; code review checklist item "is this used as a key?". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap everything in synchronized (does not fix it) nor call rehash hacks via reflection. Re-keying costs two map operations, acceptable at 800 RPS.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if keys sit in a TreeMap and the comparator field is mutated? → Same class of bug: tree ordering invariant is broken, lookups navigate the wrong subtree.
  • Can I just remove then re-add after mutation? → Only if you remove before mutating; after, remove fails.
  • Does ConcurrentHashMap help? → No. It is the same hash-at-insert behaviour.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of an incident where a request-scoped builder object was reused as a Set element, mutated downstream, and the set silently dropped membership checks; found only through a MAT query comparing stored hashes to recomputed ones.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames concurrency or the container; cannot explain the lookup failure.
  • Hire: Identifies key mutation, explains the stored hash/bucket mismatch, makes the key immutable.
  • Strong hire: Adds the MAT/heap-dump verification, the leak angle, TreeMap analogue, and a prevention rule (records, lint).

questions.subtopic: HashMap resize, load factor and iteration
questions.promptHtml: How does HashMap resize, why does the load factor default to 0.75, how should I presize one, and can I rely on its iteration order?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Performance tuning (avoiding rehash storms) and correctness (hidden order dependencies, ConcurrentModificationException) in one question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When size exceeds capacity times load factor (16 x 0.75 = 12 initially), the table doubles and entries are redistributed. Because capacity is a power of two, each entry either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCap, decided by one bit of its hash. 0.75 balances memory against collision probability. If I know the number of entries, I presize to n / 0.75 + 1, or use HashMap.newHashMap(n) since Java 19. Iteration order is unspecified and can change after a resize; if I need order, I use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Javadoc: rehash happens when entries exceed load factor x capacity, doubling the buckets; presizing with initial capacity greater than max entries / load factor guarantees no rehash.
  • Resize cost: allocate a new array of 2n and visit every node. Each chain splits into a "lo" list (stays at i) and a "hi" list (moves to i + oldCap) according to (hash & oldCap) == 0, preserving relative order. No hashCode recalculation: the hash is cached in the node.
  • Presizing arithmetic: for 1000 entries, new HashMap<>(1000) rounds to capacity 1024, threshold 768, so it still resizes at the 769th entry. Use (int)(1000 / 0.75f) + 1 = 1334 (rounds to 2048) or HashMap.newHashMap(1000) (Java 19+), which does the division for you.
  • Iteration cost is proportional to capacity + size, so an oversized, mostly-empty map iterates slowly.
  • Iteration order: not guaranteed (Javadoc). It depends on hash spread and capacity, so it changes after resize and differs across JDK versions. Set.of/Map.of (Java 9+) deliberately randomize iteration order per JVM run.
  • Fail-fast: structural modification during iteration (other than via the iterator) usually throws ConcurrentModificationException; this is best effort and only for bug detection, never a synchronization mechanism.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>((int) (expected / 0.75f) + 1);   // all Java versions
Map<String, Integer> m2 = HashMap.newHashMap(expected);                  // Java 19+

// Safe removal while iterating
m.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == 0);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• new HashMap<>(n) thinking it holds n entries without resize.
  • Writing tests that assert HashMap iteration order (flaky across JDKs).
  • Removing inside a for-each: CME (or worse, no CME when removing the second-to-last element).
  • Setting a huge initial capacity "to be safe": memory and slow iteration.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not a load factor of 1.0? → Fewer buckets but more collisions; lookup cost rises; 0.75 is a space/time compromise, not a magic value.
  2. What is the max capacity? → 2^30 buckets; beyond that threshold becomes Integer.MAX_VALUE and no more resizing.
  3. How did Java 7 resizing fail under concurrency? → Head-insert transfer could create a cycle, causing infinite loops on get; Java 8 removed that specific loop but concurrent writes still lose data.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Resizes at 75%, doubles." Senior: lo/hi split with no rehash, presizing arithmetic and the common off-by-capacity bug, iteration cost, CME is not a guarantee, and picks the right ordered map.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A batch job building a 5M-entry map by default growth paid for ~19 doublings (about 40M node touches); presizing cut the build time by a third and removed GC spikes from large array allocations.

questions.promptHtml: Compare TreeMap, PriorityQueue and ArrayDeque: data structure, complexity, ordering guarantees, and when you would pick each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are the "not HashMap" workhorses behind schedulers, top-K, sliding windows and range queries. Interviewers check for the traps (PriorityQueue iteration is not sorted, comparator consistency, nulls).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "TreeMap is a red-black tree: sorted by key, O(log n) get/put/remove, plus range operations like floorKey, subMap. PriorityQueue is a binary min-heap in an array: O(1) peek, O(log n) offer/poll, O(n) remove(Object), and iteration order is not sorted. ArrayDeque is a resizable circular array: O(1) amortized at both ends, the right default for stacks and queues, no nulls. The first thing I ask is whether I need sorted lookup (TreeMap), repeated min/max extraction (PriorityQueue) or plain FIFO/LIFO (ArrayDeque)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• TreeMap: ordering by Comparable or supplied Comparator. The comparator defines key equality (compare == 0 means same key), so an inconsistent-with-equals comparator makes it violate the Map contract. Not thread-safe; ConcurrentSkipListMap is the concurrent sorted analogue.
  • PriorityQueue: array-backed binary heap; offer sift-up, poll sift-down, both O(log n). new PriorityQueue<>(collection) heapifies in O(n). peek is O(1). Iterating or toString gives heap array order, not sorted order. No nulls. Not thread-safe (PriorityBlockingQueue is). Ties are broken arbitrarily: not stable.
  • ArrayDeque: power-of-two circular buffer with head and tail indices; no per-element node. Faster than LinkedList and Stack (legacy, synchronized). Null elements are rejected because null signals empty from poll.
TreeMap PriorityQueue ArrayDeque
core op get/put O(log n) offer/poll O(log n) add/poll ends O(1)
sorted iteration yes no insertion order
nulls no null keys (natural order) no no
range queries yes no no

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// top-K largest of a stream: min-heap of size K
PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();
for (int x : data) { heap.offer(x); if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll(); }

TreeMap<Long, String> byTime = new TreeMap<>();
var upcoming = byTime.ceilingEntry(now);           // next event at or after now
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); stack.push(1); stack.pop();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Printing a PriorityQueue and assuming sorted order.
  • Comparator subtracting ints (a - b) which overflows; use Integer.compare.
  • Using PriorityQueue.remove(obj) for cancellations in a hot path (O(n)).
  • Using TreeMap keyed by a type whose comparator ignores a field that equals uses: entries silently collapse.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why top-K with a min-heap of size K rather than sorting? → O(n log k) time, O(k) memory, works on streams.
  2. How to implement a scheduler with cancellation? → PriorityQueue with lazy deletion (flag), or TreeMap/ConcurrentSkipListMap for O(log n) removal; for timers, ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor or a timing wheel.
  3. How would you build a stable PriorityQueue? → Add a monotonically increasing sequence number as a tie-breaker in the comparator.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "TreeMap sorted, PriorityQueue for priorities." Senior: knows the heap layout and non-sorted iteration, O(n) removal, comparator-defines-equality, stability, and which concurrent alternative applies.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rate limiter used PriorityQueue.remove on every cancellation; at 50k pending timers the O(n) removals pegged a core until it moved to lazy deletion.

questions.promptHtml: How do you build an LRU cache with LinkedHashMap, and what are the limits of that approach in a real service?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic coding question, but the senior signal is knowing why it works (access order, hook method) and why it is not what you ship (thread safety, no TTL, no stats, eviction by count only).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LinkedHashMap is a HashMap whose entries are also in a doubly-linked list. With the constructor new LinkedHashMap<>(cap, 0.75f, true) the list is in access order: every get/put moves the entry to the tail. I override removeEldestEntry to return size() > max, which evicts the head, the least recently used. It is O(1) but not thread-safe, even reads mutate the structure in access-order mode, and it has no TTL or weight-based eviction, so in production I use Caffeine."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Each LinkedHashMap.Entry extends HashMap.Node with before and after pointers. HashMap provides O(1) lookup; the list provides ordering. Hooks afterNodeAccess, afterNodeInsertion, afterNodeRemoval maintain the list.
  • accessOrder=false (default) = insertion order; re-inserting an existing key does not change order. accessOrder=true makes get, getOrDefault, put (existing), compute* and merge reorder.
  • After inserting, afterNodeInsertion calls removeEldestEntry(eldest); returning true removes it.
  • Thread safety: in access-order mode get is a structural modification, so even concurrent readers corrupt the list, and iterating while another thread reads throws CME. Collections.synchronizedMap serializes everything on one lock (contention at high RPS).
  • Java 21 adds the SequencedMap interface (JEP 431) to LinkedHashMap: firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, putFirst, putLast, reversed().
  • Limits: count-based only (no byte weight), no expiry, no async load, no hit-rate stats, no protection from scan pollution (a one-time full scan evicts the hot set; Caffeine's W-TinyLFU is more scan-resistant).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Lru<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int max;
    Lru(int max) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.max = max; }
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > max; }
}
var cache = Collections.synchronizedMap(new Lru<String, byte[]>(10_000));
// production: Caffeine
Cache<String, byte[]> c = Caffeine.newBuilder().maximumSize(10_000)
        .expireAfterWrite(java.time.Duration.ofMinutes(10)).recordStats().build();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting accessOrder=true (you built a FIFO cache).
  • Sharing it across threads unsynchronized "because it is mostly reads".
  • Holding the lock while loading values from the database (stampede + serialization).
  • Treating capacity as bytes: 10k entries of 1 MB each is 10 GB.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Implement LRU without LinkedHashMap. → HashMap<K,Node> plus a doubly-linked list with sentinel head/tail; move-to-front on access.
  2. How to make it concurrent? → Don't hand-roll; Caffeine uses striped read buffers and a write buffer so reads do not take the eviction lock.
  3. What if values are large and variable-size? → Weight-based eviction (maximumWeight + weigher) or off-heap cache.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes the removeEldestEntry snippet. Senior explains the entry linkage, that reads mutate in access-order mode, the thread-safety and stampede problems, and names Caffeine with TTL/stats/admission policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A synchronized LRU in front of a product API serialized 16 request threads on one monitor; p99 dropped from 180 ms to 25 ms after moving to Caffeine.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between Collections.unmodifiableList, List.of, List.copyOf, Guava ImmutableList and a Kotlin List? Which are truly immutable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Defensive copying and API design. Many engineers believe "unmodifiable" means "immutable", and Kotlin's read-only vs immutable distinction trips even experienced people.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Collections.unmodifiableList is a read-only view: if someone holds the original list and changes it, the view changes. List.of (Java 9+) and List.copyOf and Guava ImmutableList are genuinely immutable and don't depend on the source; List.of rejects nulls. Arrays.asList is fixed-size but writable-through to the array. A Kotlin List is only a read-only interface; the object behind it may still be a mutable ArrayList. And all of these are shallow: the elements can still be mutable."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Type Mutation via this ref Backing change visible? Nulls Notes
Collections.unmodifiableList(l) throws UOE yes (view) allowed wrapper, O(1)
Arrays.asList(arr) set ok, add/remove throw yes (write-through array) allowed fixed-size
List.of(...) (9+) throws no NPE compact, value-based; contains(null) throws
List.copyOf(c) (10+) throws no NPE returns the same instance if already immutable
Stream.toList() (16+) throws no allowed unmodifiable
Guava ImmutableList throws no NPE copyOf avoids re-copying
Kotlin List<T> compile-time only yes if backed by mutable per type toList() makes a copy

Other facts:

  • Set.of/Map.of (Java 9) have randomized iteration order per JVM run (salted), so code that depends on order breaks intermittently across restarts. They also reject duplicate elements/keys at construction (IllegalArgumentException).
  • Immutable collections give thread-safe publication if the elements are immutable, and cheaper memory for small sizes.
  • Shallow immutability: List.of(new StringBuilder()) still lets you mutate the builder.
  • Kotlin: listOf() returns an immutable-ish JVM list but the type system promises nothing; casting to MutableList may work at runtime. kotlinx.collections.immutable provides persistent collections.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
List<String> src = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src);
List<String> copy = List.copyOf(src);
src.add("b");
// view -> [a, b]   copy -> [a]
val mutable = mutableListOf(1, 2)
val ro: List<Int> = mutable
mutable.add(3)            // ro now shows [1,2,3]
val safe = mutable.toList()   // snapshot copy

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning Collections.unmodifiableList(this.items) from a getter and thinking state is protected from the owner (fine for callers) but not a snapshot.
  • Using List.of with possibly-null data (NPE) or map.get results.
  • List.of(array) quirks and assuming sort works (UnsupportedOperationException on sort).
  • Exposing a Kotlin List property backed by a mutable list in a Java-callable API.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When would you pick the view over a copy? → Large collection, callers only read, owner mutates under its own lock and you want live data.
  2. Why did the JDK reject nulls in List.of? → Null-hostility avoids ambiguity and allows compact specialised implementations.
  3. How do you make a deeply immutable domain object? → Immutable collections of immutable elements (records, final fields), no setters, defensive copy in the constructor.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "unmodifiable = immutable." Senior distinguishes view/copy/fixed-size, knows null and ordering behaviour, shallowness, Kotlin read-only semantics, and designs APIs around snapshots.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A config holder returned an unmodifiable view while a reload thread swapped contents in place; readers saw half-updated lists until it was changed to publish a List.copyOf snapshot through a volatile field.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service processes order lines. A reviewer approved this change; after release, intermittent wrong totals and occasional ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException appear under load (about 300 RPS, orders of 5-2000 lines). Another report: some orders produce duplicate-key errors.

List<Line> lines = order.lines();
List<Double> prices = new ArrayList<>();

lines.parallelStream()
     .filter(l -> l.qty() > 0)
     .forEach(l -> prices.add(l.price() * l.qty()));       // (1)

Map<String, Line> bySku = lines.stream()
     .collect(Collectors.toMap(Line::sku, l -> l));        // (2)

Stream<Line> s = lines.stream().filter(Line::taxable);
long taxable = s.count();
double sum = s.mapToDouble(Line::price).sum();             // (3)

Red herring: the team suspects a JDK bug in ArrayList.
questions.promptHtml: List every defect, explain each failure mechanically, and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixes (1) by "add synchronized" and misses (2) and (3), or blames ArrayList.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can an order contain the same SKU on two lines? Is the stream pipeline latency-sensitive, and what else runs in the common pool? Are totals money (BigDecimal) or double?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert parallelStream() to a sequential stream (the bug disappears at once), roll forward the other fixes afterwards.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) shared mutable state in a parallel forEach; (2) toMap throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key on duplicates; (3) stream reuse; (4) floating-point sum ordering.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with many lines repeated in a loop (ArrayList race shows lost elements or AIOOBE); a test with duplicate SKUs; the second terminal op on a consumed stream throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Compare results sequential vs parallel.
  5. Root cause: (1) ArrayList.add is not thread-safe: concurrent threads in the common pool lose updates or overflow the backing array (the AIOOBE). The stream contract requires stateless, non-interfering lambdas. (2) toMap without a merge function throws on duplicate keys, only when data has them, hence "some orders". (3) Streams are single-use: s.count() consumes it; the next call throws. In the code as written (3) throws deterministically, so it would have failed in testing; mention it as a latent bug.
  6. Fix:
List<Double> prices = lines.stream()                    // sequential: 2000 lines does not justify parallel
    .filter(l -> l.qty() > 0)
    .map(l -> l.price() * l.qty())
    .toList();                                          // collect, don't mutate captured state

Map<String, Line> bySku = lines.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(Line::sku, l -> l, (a, b) -> a));  // explicit merge policy

List<Line> taxableLines = lines.stream().filter(Line::taxable).toList();
long taxable = taxableLines.size();
double sum = taxableLines.stream().mapToDouble(Line::price).sum();

Long-term: use BigDecimal for money. 7. Prevention: Lint rule/ErrorProne for lambdas mutating captured collections; ban parallelStream without a JMH benchmark; test with duplicate and empty inputs. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "just synchronize the list": it fixes the race but keeps a contended parallel pipeline on the shared common pool for tiny work. Not Collectors.toList() assuming mutability: toList() (16+) is unmodifiable; Collectors.toList() gives no guarantee.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would Collectors.toConcurrentMap help? → It avoids the race but still throws on duplicate keys without a merge function.
  • Is peek OK for the add? → No, peek is for debugging; with short-circuit or optimization it may not run.
  • Parallel result differs in floating sum? → Yes, double addition is not associative; parallel changes the order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a parallel forEach appended to a HashMap during nightly aggregation; results were off by 0.1% only on large tenants, which took a week to find because small-tenant tests passed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Finds only one bug or applies synchronized and calls it done.
  • Hire: Finds all three, fixes with collect/merge function, explains why.
  • Strong hire: Also covers common-pool sharing, floating-point non-associativity, BigDecimal, and a prevention lint/test strategy.

questions.promptHtml: Why are Java Strings immutable, what is the string pool, and when does intern() help or hurt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Strings dominate heap in most services. This checks memory-model understanding (safe publication, hash caching) and awareness of real tuning knobs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "String is immutable so it can be shared safely across threads, its hash can be cached, it is safe as a map key and for security-sensitive values like class names or file paths. Literals and compile-time constants are interned in the string pool, which lives in the heap since Java 7. new String("a") == "a" is false, .intern() returns the pool instance. I'd rarely call intern manually: it costs a native table lookup and can pin memory; for many duplicate strings I'd use G1 string deduplication or fix the source instead."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Fields: byte[] value, coder (LATIN1 or UTF16), cached hash. Compact strings (Java 9+) store Latin-1 text as 1 byte/char, halving memory for most data.
  • Immutability gives: safe publication via final fields (the JMM guarantees other threads see the fully built value), cached hash (a lazily computed benign race is safe because it is an idempotent int), and thread-safety with no locks.
  • String pool: a native StringTable (hash table) of interned strings. In Java 7+ it is on the heap, so interned strings can be GC'd; in Java 6 it was in PermGen. The bucket count is tunable via -XX:StringTableSize; the default has grown over versions (verify for your JDK, e.g. -XX:+PrintStringTableStatistics on Java 8 or jcmd <pid> VM.stringtable).
  • intern() can reduce memory if a high-cardinality input has very few distinct values, but it adds lookup cost, and an unbounded set of distinct interned strings bloats the table (chains get long, slowing every intern).
  • Alternatives: -XX:+UseStringDeduplication (G1 since 8u20; also in ZGC/Shenandoah in later versions, verify) dedups the backing byte[] in the background without changing identity; or an application-level Interner (Guava) with weak references.
  • == on Strings compares identity: works by accident for literals, fails for dynamically built strings.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
String a = "order";
String b = new String("order");
String c = b.intern();
System.out.println(a == b);   // false
System.out.println(a == c);   // true
System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // true
-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:+UseStringDeduplication   # background dedup of duplicate backing arrays
jcmd <pid> VM.stringtable                  # inspect the table (JDK 9+)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Comparing Strings with ==.
  • Interning user-controlled input (unbounded growth, a DoS vector).
  • Thinking final String is what makes it immutable (it is the class design).
  • Storing secrets in String: cannot be zeroed; char[] can.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is the pool in Java 6 vs 8+? → PermGen vs heap; 8 removed PermGen entirely (Metaspace is native memory).
  2. Does s1 + s2 of two literals get interned? → Constant expressions are folded and interned at compile time; runtime concatenation is not.
  3. Why is hash allowed to race? → Computing it twice yields the same int; with the value 0 treated as "not computed" it can recompute but never produce a wrong answer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Immutable for security and pool." Senior: ties it to JMM final-field publication, hash caching, compact strings, heap-based pool and its tuning, and why dedup beats manual intern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service that interned every log tag from request data saw the string table dominate GC root scanning pauses; removing intern and using dedup stabilised pauses.

questions.promptHtml: Why does Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b print true but 128 prints false? And what does autoboxing cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A beloved L1 trap, with a path to performance: allocation, null unboxing NPE, and primitive vs boxed in hot code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Autoboxing compiles to Integer.valueOf, which returns cached instances for -128..127 (guaranteed by the Javadoc), so == on identical small values compares the same object. Outside the range it may allocate a new object, so == compares different references. Always use equals for boxed types. Boxing also costs an allocation (16 bytes for an Integer with compressed oops), extra pointer chasing, and a null can NPE on unboxing."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Integer.valueOf(int) caches -128..127; the Javadoc says it always caches that range and may cache more. The upper bound is adjustable with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=<n> (HotSpot) / java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high; treat as an implementation detail. Long, Short, Byte, Character (0..127) and Boolean have caches too; Double and Float have none.
  • new Integer(5) is deprecated for removal (since 9, marked for removal in 16): always allocates.
  • Cost: Integer object = 12 B header + 4 B value = 16 B. List<Integer> of n elements costs about 4 B ref + 16 B object = 20 B per element vs 4 B for int[]. Reads go through a pointer: cache misses on large lists.
  • Escape analysis can remove some boxes in compiled code, but it is not reliable across collections, megamorphic calls or large methods.
  • Unboxing a null throws NPE: Integer x = map.get(k); int y = x;. Ternaries mixing int and Integer can unbox unexpectedly: cond ? 1 : nullInteger NPEs.
  • Overload trap: list.remove(int index) vs remove(Object o) with List<Integer>.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Integer a = 127, b = 127;  System.out.println(a == b);       // true
Integer c = 128, d = 128;  System.out.println(c == d);       // false (typical)
System.out.println(c.equals(d));                              // true

List<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
l.remove(1);                    // removes index 1 -> [10, 30]
l.remove(Integer.valueOf(10));  // removes the value 10
val a: Int? = 128; val b: Int? = 128
println(a == b)    // true (structural)
println(a === b)   // false (identity on boxed)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• == between Integer/Long in business logic (works in tests with small ids, breaks in prod with large ids).
  • Long total = 0L; for (...) total += x; allocating a Long every iteration.
  • Map<String, Integer>.get() assigned to int without null check.
  • Trusting the cache bound as a spec.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why cache -128..127? → Small values are very common (byte range); the JLS requires boxing to give identical objects for that range.
  2. How do you avoid boxing in hot code? → Primitive arrays, IntStream, Map<K,Integer>.merge still boxes; use fastutil/Eclipse Collections primitive maps.
  3. Does == on Integer vs int compare references? → No: mixed operands unbox to numeric comparison.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Cache up to 127." Senior: Javadoc-guaranteed range vs implementation, object size math, null-unboxing NPE, collection memory overhead, remove overload, and the Kotlin == vs === difference.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service compared Long user ids with ==; it worked for ids < 128 in staging and silently failed in prod for most users.

questions.contextHtml:
An internal pricing API on 4 vCPU pods (heap 2 GB, G1) normally serves 1,200 RPS at p99 40 ms. After a deploy that introduced an in-memory index Map<RouteKey, Quote> with about 300k entries, p99 climbs to 6 s within an hour of warmup; CPU sits at 100%. GC logs are normal (young pauses 15 ms, no Full GC). Thread dumps show 30+ threads RUNNABLE in:

at java.base/java.util.HashMap$TreeNode.find(HashMap.java:...)
at java.base/java.util.HashMap$TreeNode.getTreeNode(HashMap.java:...)
at java.base/java.util.HashMap.get(HashMap.java:...)
at com.acme.pricing.RouteIndex.lookup(RouteIndex.java:41)

Key class: record-like final class RouteKey(String origin, String dest, int serviceLevel) with hashCode() { return serviceLevel; } (author reasoned "equals compares all three, hash needs only be consistent"). serviceLevel takes 5 values. Red herring: the team wants to increase heap and switch to ZGC.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix it, and explain why Java 8+ treeification did not save you.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap, tune GC" or "use ConcurrentHashMap". Misses that CPU is in HashMap itself and that the hash function degenerates to 5 distinct values.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did latency track map size (it grew over warmup)? Is GC time flat? Which key classes go into this map? What does hashCode look like? Is the map read-only after load?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the deploy or feature-flag the index off and fall back to the prior lookup; scale out only as a stopgap since every pod has the same bug.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) degenerate hashCode (5 distinct values over 300k keys, ~60k keys per bucket); (b) GC pressure (ruled out by logs); (c) thread contention (threads are RUNNABLE on CPU, not BLOCKED); (d) JIT deopt.
  4. How I'd verify each: async-profiler/JFR CPU flame graph showing TreeNode.find; jstack x3 confirms same frames; a quick test computing the distinct count of key.hashCode() over a sample (stream.map(hashCode).distinct().count()); GC log -Xlog:gc* to rule out (b).
  5. Root cause: hashCode returns one of 5 values, so ~60k keys share each bucket. HashMap treeified the bins (>=8 entries, table >= 64), but RouteKey is not Comparable, so the tree can order only by hash (all equal), then tieBreakOrder (identity hash). find cannot know which subtree holds the key and must search both, degrading to a linear scan, now with tree-node pointer chasing. So lookups are O(n/5) per call, 60k equals comparisons.
  6. Fix: a proper hash, and optionally make the key Comparable as defence in depth:
record RouteKey(String origin, String dest, int serviceLevel) {}   // generated hashCode uses all components

or Objects.hash(origin, dest, serviceLevel). Short term: ship the one-line hash fix; also presize the map. 7. Prevention: a unit test asserting hash distribution (e.g. >= 0.9 x n distinct hashes for a sample); prefer records; ErrorProne/IDE inspection for hashCode ignoring equals fields; load test with production-size cardinality before release (a 1k-entry test would hide it). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "move to ZGC" (CPU-bound, not GC); not ConcurrentHashMap (same bucket structure). Making the key Comparable adds an ordering contract to maintain; I'd do it only if keys may be attacker-influenced.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would Strings as keys have been safe? → Mostly: String is Comparable, so a collision-heavy bin degrades to O(log n) instead of O(n).
  • What if attacker-supplied keys collide deliberately? → Same pattern; Comparable keys limit damage to O(log n), plus input size limits (max params/headers) and per-request key caps.
  • How would you detect this class of bug in CI? → A microbenchmark (JMH) at realistic cardinality; hash-distribution assertions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team "optimised" a composite key's hashCode to use only the tenant id to speed up hashing; a 40x slowdown showed up only after a big tenant onboarded, and the flame graph was 85% HashMap.get.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Tunes heap/GC, no hashCode insight.
  • Hire: Spots the degenerate hash from the stack trace, fixes hashCode, explains buckets.
  • Strong hire: Explains why treeification can't help without Comparable, gives verification (flame graph, distinct-hash test), prevention tests, and the attack-input angle.

questions.promptHtml: When do streams cost more than loops, and when is parallelStream() actually a good idea in a server application?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates "functional style is cleaner" from knowing the runtime cost model and the shared-pool hazard that has caused real outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A stream pipeline allocates lambda/stage objects and, for object streams, boxes primitives. The JIT usually inlines it well for monomorphic hot code, but in cold or megamorphic paths a loop wins, and the overhead matters only at tight inner loops or tiny workloads. Parallel streams split work across the single JVM-wide common ForkJoinPool, so in a server they let one request's CPU-heavy or blocking work starve others. I use them rarely: large CPU-bound data, good splittability (arrays, ArrayList, ranges), no blocking, no shared state, and only after a JMH benchmark."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Pipeline = source -> intermediate ops -> terminal op. It is lazy: nothing runs until the terminal op; ops fuse into one pass per element (a stateless filter+map), but stateful ops (sorted, distinct) buffer.
  • Costs: stage objects per pipeline, a captured lambda allocation if it captures variables, Spliterator overhead, boxing for Stream<Integer> (use IntStream/mapToInt). For a 10-element list, setup cost dominates.
  • JIT: the terminal loop calls the stage chain via interface calls; if the same pipeline code path is used with many different lambdas, the call site becomes megamorphic and inlining fails.
  • Stream.iterate/LinkedList/TreeSet sources split poorly in parallel.
  • Parallel streams: use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() with parallelism usually cores - 1; the calling thread participates. One pool for the whole JVM (incl. other libraries and CompletableFuture async defaults). A blocking call in a parallel stream occupies carrier workers and stalls everything else that uses the pool. findFirst, limit, forEachOrdered impose ordering overhead. Running inside a custom ForkJoinPool via pool.submit(() -> stream.parallel()...) is a widely used workaround but depends on implementation detail and is not documented behaviour.
  • Rule of thumb from the stream docs: parallel helps when N x Q (elements x cost per element) is large (rough guide: tens of thousands of simple operations or heavier work), but measure.
  • In containers, availableProcessors() follows the cgroup CPU limit, so a 2-CPU pod gets a pool of 1 worker plus the caller.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// boxing cost: avoid Stream<Integer> in hot paths
long sum = IntStream.range(0, n).filter(i -> i % 3 == 0).asLongStream().sum();

// risky in a server: blocking IO on the shared pool
orders.parallelStream().forEach(o -> httpClient.send(o));   // starves the common pool
// Kotlin: sequences vs lists; inline collection functions create no lambda objects
val total = items.asSequence().filter { it.active }.sumOf { it.price }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Parallel = faster" without a benchmark (often slower for small N or I/O).
  • Doing I/O or DB calls inside a parallel stream.
  • Mutating shared state in lambdas.
  • Using sorted() or distinct() on huge streams unknowingly (full buffering).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you size the common pool? → -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N; global, affects all users of the pool.
  2. Do virtual threads change this? → Blocking per-element work belongs on an executor of virtual threads, not a parallel stream (see virtual threads sections).
  3. Why do Kotlin collection operations differ? → Inline functions avoid lambda allocation, but each eager step creates an intermediate list; asSequence is lazy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Parallel streams use multiple cores." Senior: cost model, boxing, megamorphic inlining, splittability, the shared common pool as a fleet-wide blast radius, and benchmark-first discipline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A report endpoint used parallelStream with a database call per item; one slow request occupied all common-pool workers and unrelated CompletableFuture.supplyAsync calls queued behind it, spiking p99 service-wide.

questions.contextHtml: A fraud-feature service keeps Map<Long, Long> (accountId -> lastEventEpochMs) in memory. It holds 10 million entries on a 4 GB heap (pods limited to 6 GB RAM, G1). Live set after GC is about 2.6 GB, and old-gen collections are frequent: young GC every 4 s, mixed collections up to 120 ms, p99 request latency 90 ms vs a target of 30 ms. The map is built once at startup then updated at about 20k writes/s, read at 60k reads/s. The team wants to cut the heap rather than add pods. Red herring: someone proposes -XX:+UseCompressedOops (already enabled at 4 GB) and G1 tuning flags.
questions.promptHtml: Where does the memory go, what would you change, and what are the risks?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap to 8 GB and use ZGC", or "use a ConcurrentHashMap". Does not do the per-entry arithmetic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the key space dense/numeric ranges? Do we need concurrent writes? Is exact recency required or can reads be slightly stale? Can ids be bounded or hashed? Does anything iterate the whole map?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise young-gen sizing / region size only as a stopgap; the real fix is shrinking the live set.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-entry object overhead (boxing + Node); (b) table resize garbage; (c) concurrency wrapper overhead; (d) leak (entries never removed).
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap histogram jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram showing java.lang.Long, HashMap$Node, Object[] counts; JOL (org.openjdk.jol) to print layouts; MAT dominator tree; GC logs -Xlog:gc* for live-set-after-GC trend.
  5. Root cause: Math per entry (compressed oops, 64-bit JVM): HashMap.Node = 12 header + 4 hash + 4 key ref + 4 value ref + 4 next ref = 28, padded to 32 B. Two Long objects = 12 header + 8 value = 20, padded to 24 B each = 48 B. Table slot about 4 B / 0.75 load, roughly 5 B on average (more right after growth). Total about 85 B/entry. 10M x 85 B = about 850 MB of retained data for 160 MB of real payload (10M x 16 B). My measured 2.6 GB suggests more: other data, a ConcurrentHashMap overhead or a recent resize; I'd confirm with the histogram (flagging that I'm using estimates).
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: presize (HashMap.newHashMap(11_000_000) on 19+) so there is no resize garbage; remove expired entries.
    • Long term: primitive open-addressing map, e.g. fastutil Long2LongOpenHashMap or Eclipse Collections LongLongHashMap: two long[] arrays, load factor about 0.5-0.75, so about 16 B / load = 21-32 B per entry, roughly 210-320 MB for 10M entries, and it is two large arrays (humongous objects in G1: size them knowing region size) with no per-entry objects, which also cuts GC marking work drastically.
    • Alternative: off-heap (Chronicle Map) or an external store (Redis) if sharing across pods matters.
  7. Prevention: Memory budget per entry in design docs; JOL-based test of the footprint; histogram alert on Long instance count; JMH comparing get/put.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Primitive maps are usually not thread-safe: I would shard by key into N maps with striped locks or write via a single owner thread with a read-optimised snapshot. Adds a third-party dependency and different API (default return value 0 for missing keys: needs containsKey/sentinel). I would not just add heap: bigger live sets mean longer concurrent marking and mixed collections.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Large long[] in G1? → Allocations >= half a region size are humongous and go directly to old gen; pick -XX:G1HeapRegionSize accordingly or use many smaller arrays.
  • What about Long cache? → Only -128..127; useless here.
  • Valhalla? → Value classes (JEP 401, preview, verify status in the JDK you use) aim to remove identity/header overhead but are not a production option yet.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team replaced Map<Integer,Integer> of 50M entries with an Eclipse Collections primitive map and went from a 9 GB to a 1.2 GB heap, and mixed-GC pauses dropped from 400 ms to under 50 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds memory/changes GC without sizing the data.
  • Hire: Does the per-entry arithmetic, proposes primitive maps, names histogram/JOL.
  • Strong hire: Adds concurrency strategy, humongous allocation caveat, API semantics (missing key default), and measures before and after.

questions.promptHtml: When do you need StringBuilder, and what does + on Strings compile to? Is StringBuffer ever the right choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of what the compiler does (changed in Java 9) and the classic O(n^2) loop trap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Since String is immutable, each concatenation produces a new String. A single expression like a + b + c is fine. Before Java 9, javac compiled it into a StringBuilder chain; from Java 9 it emits an invokedynamic call to StringConcatFactory (JEP 280), which can size the result exactly. Concatenation inside a loop is the problem: each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, giving O(n^2). Use one StringBuilder (preferably presized) outside the loop. StringBuffer is the synchronized legacy variant; I almost never use it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Per concatenation: allocate a new byte[] of the combined length and copy. In a loop of n appends producing length L, total copying is O(n x L).
  • Java 8 and earlier: javac translates a + b into new StringBuilder().append(a).append(b).toString(). In a loop, a new builder per iteration.
  • Java 9+ (JEP 280): invokedynamic bootstrap picks a strategy at link time (default: compute lengths, allocate a single exact-size array, no intermediate builder). The strategy can be switched via a javac option for experiments. A concatenation in a loop still re-copies the accumulating string.
  • StringBuilder is a growable char/byte array (capacity default 16; growth about 2x + 2). Presize if you know the length: new StringBuilder(n).
  • StringBuffer synchronizes every method; per-call locking buys nothing since a builder is almost never shared across threads, and it could not make compound operations atomic anyway.
  • String.join, Collectors.joining, and String.format (slow: parses the pattern each time) are alternatives; text blocks (Java 15) for literals.
  • String.concat and += on null prints "null".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// O(n^2): each += copies the growing string
String s = "";
for (String p : parts) s += p;

// O(n)
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(parts.size() * 8);
for (String p : parts) sb.append(p).append(',');
String out = sb.toString();

String joined = String.join(",", parts);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building SQL/JSON by concatenating user input (injection) rather than binding parameters.
  • Concatenating inside a log call that is disabled: log.debug("x" + expensive()) builds the string anyway; use parameterized logging.
  • Using StringBuffer "for thread safety" in shared code.
  • Calling sb.toString() repeatedly in a loop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is + in a loop always slow? → Yes asymptotically; for tiny n the difference is negligible, but a loop can hide a growing n.
  2. Why did Java 9 change the translation? → Smaller bytecode, no builder allocation hierarchy, and the runtime can optimise strategies without recompiling classes.
  3. How would you build a 100 MB payload? → Stream to an output (writer/OutputStream), not a single String.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use StringBuilder in loops." Senior: states the indy change (JEP 280), exact-size allocation, O(n^2) mechanics, presizing, parameterized logging, and streaming for large outputs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An export job doing csv += row for 200k rows took minutes and 30 GB/s allocation; a StringBuilder (then a streaming writer) cut it to seconds.

questions.promptHtml: How expensive are exceptions in Java, where does the cost come from, and when is it acceptable to throw them in a hot path?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The "exceptions are slow" claim is half-true. Seniors can say exactly which part is expensive, how the JIT treats it, and the surprising OmitStackTraceInFastThrow behaviour.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Creating a Throwable is the expensive part, because the constructor calls fillInStackTrace, a native stack walk whose cost grows with stack depth. Unwinding to a handler costs less, and a try block that does not throw is essentially free. So deep stacks in frameworks make throwing costly; a stackless exception (override fillInStackTrace or use the four-argument constructor with writableStackTrace=false) is cheap, and when the JIT inlines throw and catch into the same compiled method it can turn the throw into a jump. Control-flow exceptions in hot paths are still a smell."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Shipilev's "Exceptional performance" benchmark: most of the cost is stack trace capture at instantiation, and that scales with depth; the rest is stack unwinding. With stack capture disabled the gap to a normal return narrows a lot (consult the post for numbers and run your own JMH).
  • Try/catch itself is zero-cost on the happy path in HotSpot: handlers are tables in compiled code, not executed instructions. Exceptions don't block inlining.
  • Cheap exceptions:
class NotFound extends RuntimeException {
    NotFound(String m) { super(m, null, false, false); }  // enableSuppression=false, writableStackTrace=false
}
  • Throwable.getStackTrace() materialises StackTraceElement[] lazily on first call: logging a full trace costs again (formatting, many lines of output, I/O).
  • -XX:+OmitStackTraceInFastThrow (on by default in C2): after an implicit exception (NPE, ArrayIndexOutOfBounds, ArithmeticException, ClassCast, ArrayStore) has been thrown many times from the same hot compiled site, the JVM reuses a preallocated exception with no stack trace. Production symptom: logs suddenly show java.lang.NullPointerException with an empty trace. Disable with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow when debugging.
  • Checked vs unchecked has no performance difference; it is a design question.
  • Exceptions across thread pools: wrapped (ExecutionException, CompletionException), each adding another stack.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Anti-pattern: exception for control flow in a hot path
try { Integer.parseInt(s); isNum = true; } catch (NumberFormatException e) { isNum = false; }

// Better: validate without throwing
boolean isNum = !s.isEmpty() && s.chars().allMatch(Character::isDigit);
-XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow     # keep traces for repeated implicit exceptions

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming try/catch is slow on the happy path.
  • Logging the same exception with a full trace 10k times per second (the log, not the throw, becomes the bottleneck).
  • Confusing "stack trace missing in logs" with a logging bug when it is the fast-throw optimisation.
  • Reusing a single preallocated exception instance: the trace points to the wrong place.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does cost scale with depth? → fillInStackTrace walks every frame, and a Spring/servlet stack can be 100+ frames deep.
  2. When is a stackless exception acceptable? → Internal control flow with a known catch site (parsers, backtracking, short-circuiting a visitor), never for failures that people debug.
  3. How do you find exception hot spots? → JFR jdk.JavaExceptionThrow / jdk.JavaErrorThrow events (disabled by default, enable them), and flame graphs showing fillInStackTrace.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Exceptions are slow, avoid them." Senior: locates the cost in stack capture and depth, knows try is free, stackless constructors, JIT inlining, the fast-throw trap, and JFR to measure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A gateway that threw a NotFoundException per cache miss at 15k/s spent 20% CPU in fillInStackTrace through a 140-frame stack; returning Optional on that path removed the cost.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review for a payment-capture outage. A nightly settlement job (30k payments, 4 worker threads) reported "SUCCESS" while 1,100 payments were never captured. Findings in the code:

public void settle(List<Payment> batch) {
    for (Payment p : batch) {
        try {
            gateway.capture(p);            // throws GatewayException (checked) or TimeoutException
        } catch (Exception e) {
            log.error("capture failed");   // no id, no cause, no stack
        }
    }
}

public Payment load(long id) {
    try { return repo.find(id); }
    catch (SQLException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e.getMessage()); }  // cause dropped
}

Also: a finally { return status; } block in the outer run() swallowed an OutOfMemoryError from a worker, and the on-call saw only "capture failed" 1,100 times with no ids. Red herring: management blames the payment gateway.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review: what is wrong in the exception handling, what do you change, and what standards do you set?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Log better and retry." Misses swallowed errors turning failures into success, lost causes, return-in-finally, catching Exception/Error, and the lack of failure accounting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the job's contract say: all-or-nothing or best effort with a report? Which failures are retryable? Is capture idempotent (idempotency key)? Who consumes the success status?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Re-run settlement for the 1,100 uncaptured payments (identify them by status in the DB, not logs), using idempotency keys to prevent double capture; page finance about timing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) swallowed exceptions mask failure; (b) transient gateway timeouts treated as terminal; (c) OOM in a worker swallowed; (d) gateway degradation (real but secondary).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare DB payment status vs job output; search logs for "capture failed" counts per hour; thread dump/heap analysis for the OOM (heap dump on OOM -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError); gateway metrics to bound the actual error rate.
  5. Root cause: The loop catches Exception and only logs a constant string: no payment id, no exception object, no counter, no failure propagation. The job's final status is computed from "did the loop finish", not "did every item succeed". Elsewhere new RuntimeException(e.getMessage()) discarded the cause and trace, and return inside finally overrides any thrown exception, including Errors, silently converting a crash into success.
  6. Fix:
public SettleResult settle(List<Payment> batch) {
    var failed = new ArrayList<FailedPayment>();
    for (Payment p : batch) {
        try {
            gateway.capture(p);
        } catch (GatewayException | TimeoutException e) {
            log.error("capture failed paymentId={}", p.id(), e);   // id + cause
            failed.add(new FailedPayment(p.id(), e));
        }
    }
    return new SettleResult(batch.size(), failed);   // caller decides: alert if failed non-empty
}

try { return repo.find(id); }
catch (SQLException e) { throw new RepositoryException("find payment " + id, e); } // wrap, keep cause

Never catch Throwable/Error to continue; never return in finally. Bounded retry with backoff on TimeoutException only, guarded by idempotency keys. 7. Prevention: Job status derived from per-item results with metrics (success/failed counters, alert on failed > 0); lint/Sonar rules: no empty or log-only catch of Exception, no return in finally, no exception wrapping without cause; a test that injects gateway failure and asserts a non-success status; structured logs with ids; heap dump on OOM and fail-fast process exit on Errors. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not fail the entire batch on one bad payment (poison item blocks 29,999 others): continue and report. Not retry blindly without idempotency (double captures). Not use checked exceptions everywhere just to force handling; domain-specific exceptions at layer boundaries are enough.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does finally { return x; } hide exceptions? → The return discards the in-flight exception; javac warns with -Xlint:finally.
  • Where does try-with-resources suppress? → The primary exception is kept, close() failures are attached via addSuppressed.
  • Checked vs unchecked for this API? → Checked for recoverable domain failures callers must decide on; unchecked for programming errors; Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so document failures in types (Result, sealed class).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite review where a "successful" nightly reconciliation hid 3% failures for five weeks; the fix that mattered was making the job's exit status a function of per-item outcomes, not any logging improvement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests more logging and retries only.
  • Hire: Identifies swallowed exceptions, lost causes and return-in-finally; proposes per-item result reporting.
  • Strong hire: Adds idempotency for re-runs, failure accounting/alerting, Error handling policy, lint rules, and the poison-item trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: What do records and sealed types give you, what are their limits, and how do they change domain modelling compared with POJOs/Lombok (and Kotlin data/sealed classes)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Modern Java fluency and design judgement: do you know the semantics (shallow immutability, generated equals) and where they bite (arrays, JPA, serialization)?

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A record (final in Java 16) is a transparent, shallowly immutable data carrier: its components define the canonical constructor, accessors, and equals/hashCode/toString. A sealed type (final in Java 17) lists its permitted subtypes, so the compiler knows the hierarchy is closed. Together with pattern-matching switch (final in 21) I get algebraic data types with exhaustiveness checks: add a subtype and every switch that misses it fails to compile. Limits: records are shallow, so a List or array component is still mutable; they can't extend classes; and most ORMs want mutable entities, so records suit DTOs and value objects, not JPA entities."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Record: record Money(long cents, String currency) {}. Implicitly final, extends java.lang.Record, fields are private final. Compact constructor validates or normalises: Money { if (cents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }. Can implement interfaces, have static members, and extra methods; cannot declare instance fields beyond components.
  • Equality: component-wise equals (using Objects.equals / primitive compare); array components compare by reference. Defensive copy lists in the compact constructor: items = List.copyOf(items).
  • Sealed: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}; each permitted subtype must be final, sealed or non-sealed. Permitted types must be in the same module/package (or same compilation unit with no permits clause).
  • Exhaustive switch over a sealed hierarchy with no default:
sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {}
record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {}
record Err<T>(String msg) implements Result<T> {}

static <T> String show(Result<T> r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Ok<T> ok -> "ok " + ok.value();
        case Err<T> err -> "err " + err.msg();
    };
}
  • Why avoid default: with it, adding a subtype compiles silently and falls into the default branch. Without it, you get a compile error.
  • Kotlin analogues: data class (copy(), componentN; mutable var allowed), sealed class/interface with exhaustive when.
  • Serialization: Jackson 2.12+ supports records; Java serialization of records is by canonical constructor. JPA entities need a no-arg constructor and mutability, so records are not entities (embeddables/projections are possible; check your Hibernate version).
  • Compatibility: adding a component changes the canonical constructor, binary-breaking for callers.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing a record is deeply immutable.
  • Putting an array component in a record and relying on equals.
  • Adding default -> to an exhaustive switch and losing compiler protection.
  • Using records as JPA entities or as cache keys with mutable components.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a record extend a class? → No (it implicitly extends Record); it can implement interfaces.
  2. Sealed vs enum? → Enum = fixed set of instances; sealed = fixed set of types, each can carry different data.
  3. Does exhaustiveness hold across modules and versions? → Only as of compile time; separately compiled callers see MatchException/IncompatibleClassChangeError risk if the hierarchy changes (verify behaviour for your JDK), so close hierarchies to public API changes carefully.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Records are concise POJOs." Senior: shallow immutability and defensive copies, equality semantics, exhaustive switch without default as a design tool, ORM/serialization limits, and API evolution cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team modelled events as a sealed interface with records; adding a new event type broke compilation in 7 switch sites, exactly where behaviour was missing, instead of surfacing as a runtime "unknown event" in production.

questions.contextHtml: A Kotlin/Java monolith exposes OrderService.getItems(): List<Item> backed by a mutable ArrayList inside an Order object cached in a Caffeine cache (200k orders, 30 min TTL). Symptoms in production at 2,500 RPS: occasionally an order shows items from another request's mutation; ConcurrentModificationException in the pricing module about 3x/hour; a stack trace shows ArrayList$Itr.checkForComodification. A recent module added discount logic that calls items.removeIf(...) on the returned list. You want to make Order safe without a flag day: 14 downstream callers (some Java, some Kotlin) and two other teams.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose it and migrate the API to safe collection exposure under live traffic?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the method synchronized" or "return a new ArrayList each time everywhere immediately." Misses that the cached object is shared across requests, that Kotlin List doesn't prevent mutation, and the need for a staged migration.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
